The results show that even a composite materials model with a high degree of uncertainty can be managed effectively by the proposed technique, enabling the practical application of precise damage prevention methods.

We're exploring the possibility that there's a reverse relationship between the sophistication of individual elements in a coalition game and the overall strategic intelligence required to thrive within that framework. To examine this hypothesis, we're reviewing research on noncooperative approaches to solving coalition games, particularly those involving complex, interrelated state spaces. By analyzing these research findings, we're seeking to identify potential counterexamples that contradict our hypothesis and provide a more in-depth understanding of the factors influencing the complexity of these games.

This research paper proposes a tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector techniques and illustrates the method's efficacy through a variety of vector identities proved using this framework.

Light particles at TeV energies that participate in electroweak interactions yet evade detection due to weak coupling can possess unusual flavor properties. If these particles improperly convert gluons to massive particles like fermions or bosons, they would significantly impact two experiments: the QCD pillar of the LHC and the deep-inelastic scattering phenomenon observed in the Deep Inelastic Scattering experiment. Consequently, researchers must ensure any theoretical models incorporating these phenomena are also compatible with the accurate values of certain electromagnetic and strong forces properties of fundamental particles. A hypothetical model involving a complex scalar field that exhibits unusual flavor properties and results in a specific reaction occurring instead of a more common one has been explored. This model has been tested against which constraints it must comply with, including multiple LHC safety nets and the precise values of certain particle property measurements.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a more intricate structure of conformal sliver states. In this paper, we focus on the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory to develop the concept of conformal sliver states further. We establish a set of Ward identities that characterize the conformal sliver states within this specific theory framework. Our analysis also reveals a novel type of ward identity not present in Liouville conformal field theory.

We demonstrate that Coxeter groups, which are equipped with a specific generating set, possess bi-automatic properties. This includes both left and right automatic aspects. This discovery results from a connection established between Coxeter groups and certain graph groups, for which a supporting framework has been previously established by Bestvina, Fei, and Horoward. Specifically, it shows that both left and right automatic aspects of a graph group are equivalent given its branch length can be minimized through a sequence of twisting operations and edge collapses, respectively.

An important step toward creating effective neural prosthetics for ambulatory purposes involves understanding the relationship between the visual cortex's neural signals and the rates at which prosthetic legs move. In contrast to recent studies focusing on connections between the cortex and electric motors, this work investigates this relationship within the central nervous system itself, without the influence of external devices, thereby providing a more fundamental understanding of how the brain controls walking speed through specific neural states. To achieve this, researchers analyzed records of neural activity from the brains of individuals with spinal cord injuries who were able to walk using a treadmill and hip-knee joint recordings, and through a complex analysis of these signals, uncovered distinct neural states corresponding to forward walking, standing, and step initiation, and consistently found that the duration of these states influenced walking speed. Specifically, shorter state durations were associated with faster walking speeds, which was also reflected in the recruitment of certain neural states at lower speeds similar to those observed in individuals without spinal cord injuries. These key discoveries about the relationships between neural states, their durations, and walking speed could have important implications for the development of effective neural controls for ambulatory purposes.

If we take a right-angled Artin group with a tree that is not a line, and a partition of its vertex set into two disjoint subsets, then there exist subgroups of its left action on a associated complex that commute with each other, and whose right-invariant points under the left action form two distinct stars, provided that the group acts freely on the complex.

Connecting nodes in a graph based on time-series data can be a powerful way to capture functional relationships, but the computational cost of existing methods makes it impractical for large datasets. Connectome Wasserstein Distance (CWD) is an effective method for modeling the connectivity of complex systems using Euler charactristics, but it requires an excessive 12 days to process 1000 datasets on a single GPU. We address this challenge by training a novel UNet-style model, Connectivity Estimator Network (CEN), which directly predicts the connectivity matrix from raw time-series data. CEN reduces connectivity estimation to a task that can be completed in less than 1 second for a single dataset on the same GPU. When applied to heart rate variability data, CEN outperforms CWD in classification accuracy. We open-source CEN at https://github.com/ghaleei/CEN.

An organism's movement through its environment is a basic indicator of its existence, and by analyzing this movement, biologists can gather valuable information about evolution, behavior, and ecology. Researchers are using a growing amount of video data to supplement and replace traditional observational methods. However, processing and interpreting this visual data automatically poses significant challenges. A key issue is that even with a large amount of data, the scale can make it difficult to identify patterns and trends related to specific organisms. Another problem arises when analyzing small organisms like plankton, where the resolution is insufficient to distinguish the organism itself. A new method is proposed to address these challenges by developing a computational approach that automatically extracts the spatial location of organisms within video frames, using a combination of machine learning-based techniques and low-level image processing. This method can adapt to various organisms and environments, and even extends to certain cases where the organism is difficult to discern from the surrounding environment. By generating a range of movement attributes related to speed, acceleration, and orientation, this method provides biologists with a valuable tool for analyzing the behavior and ecology of organisms based on video data, and can be applied to a wide range of biological studies.

The project involves creating a highly efficient iterative matrix inversion algorithm, capable of handling complex systems of nonlinear equations with multiple variables. To achieve this, we draw upon concepts from Newton's method, fusion techniques, and weighted recursive least squares, incorporating them into an iterative framework. The algorithm's iterative nature makes it well-suited for large-scale matrix inversion tasks by minimizing memory usage, whereas its efficiency in terms of computational time is optimized through a balanced selection of tuning parameters. Furthermore, the algorithm's modular design enables seamless integration with different resolution control methods, ensuring numerical stability is maintained during the convergence process. The project involves providing C GPU code for matrix inversion and C CPU code for systems of nonlinear equations, along with a Python API for easy integration.

We investigate topological phases in one-dimensional conductors with spatially correlated random disorders. This study extends previous research on the topological properties of clean and statistically uniform disordered systems. Numerical results show that the topological phase is influenced by both the correlation length and the strength of the random disorders. Our findings indicate that the topological phase can be protected by creating a spatial gradient of the disorder correlations, which is relevant to experimental situations. Moreover, we found that the topological phase boundaries match the analytical results from a theoretical approach based on the weak disorder approximation, which is valid when the disorder strength is minimal. Our proposed model, which we call the topological Anderson conductor, offers potential for realizing a topologically stable phase in real systems.

We introduce a type of graph-based rewriting system called CPM (Cartesian Proof Method) systems, which comprise disks connected by arcs, and a corresponding algorithm for proving implications about the behavior of discrete systems. We demonstrate how both the basic framework and the proof algorithm can be implemented using simple cuts, which represent a way to reinterpret the underlying geometry. By applying these tools to a specific problem, we show the process and resulting strategy for solving it.

We've developed an efficient and accurate method for creating on-shell Higgs boson masses in the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, considering complex parameters and their impact, and we've made this method available for theoretical predictions beyond the Tevatron and LEP limits.

Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and it has been extensively studied in the single-agent setting. However, research in the dual-agent setting is less common, especially when agents have distinct context sets without knowledge sharing. In this scenario, defining a meaningful context that accounts for distinct sets is crucial. We establish a lower bound of approximately 197 context dimensions, which is a specific number for now, in order to efficiently learn a linear bandit context of that size without knowledge sharing. We achieve this goal with a novel algorithm called Distributed Linear Context Bandit (DLCB) that uses approximately 12 times the square root of the target regret as data dimensions in context estimation and approximately 395 times the target regret in context size in parameter estimation. DLCB is applicable to agents with varying context sets.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency via distributionally resilient optimization. Building upon this, we highlight the importance of accounting for confounding variables and selection biases in order to achieve accurate estimation of treatment effects via machine learning methods. Although widely practiced, this assumption is often violated in real-world settings, leading to flawed policy recommendations. Our results demonstrate that through careful selection of averaging weights, behavioral learning under stochastic approximation can result in policy recommendations that are resilient to distributions shifts and yield optimal expected outcomes.

Our study introduces a new method to manipulate event shapes by re-weighing events by a function of the participant plane angles, allowing for a more precise measurement of elliptic flow ($v_2$) at low transverse momentum.  By re-weighing events for specific ranges of the initial geometry, our approach helps disentangle the contributions of different flow harmonics on particle distributions.  Utilizing ALICE data from Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_\rm{NN}}=2.76$ TeV, our analysis reveals that a second-order event shape weight centered on the second most dominant participant plane angle generally yields smaller uncertainties for $v_2$ than traditional methods.  These findings hold true for both charged hadrons and pions.  Additionally, our results indicate that the average initial ellipticity decreases with increasing impact parameter, a trend that may be understood through the incorporation of fluctuations in the initial geometry.  Our research also highlights the importance of considering fluctuations in geometry when interpreting the results of collective flow.

This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal extremal GDoF differences resulting from optimal versus binary power control in large interference networks. Initial research in extremal network theory investigates the extremes of performance or capacity in networks, whereas GDoF analyses focus on the maximal data transfer rates in an interference network, taking into account power constraints and ideal interference cancellation. When examining the extremal differences in GDoF, we find that in networks with multiple users, the difference in extremal GDoF caused by optimal versus binary power control can vary greatly, ranging from 0 to a significant number, and is directly influenced by the number of users. Furthermore, we establish that the extremal extremal GDoF difference caused by these two power control methods is directly proportional to the square root of the number of users and can be any value within the range from approximately 2.5 times the square root of the number of users to infinity.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration method utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our method was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our method reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy.

This research paper investigates the positive integer values of $a, b, $ and $n$ for which the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ holds true. We begin by examining a related quadratic equation, solve for its factors, and then use these solutions to establish conditions for $a, b, $ and $n$. These conditions enable us to derive a criterion that can be applied to either $v_7(a)$ or $v_7(b)$, leading to a sequence of possible values for either $a$ or $b$. We then examine two cases based on the values of $a$ or $b$ modulo $7$, and for each case, we determine the corresponding values of $n$. Should $a$ or $b$ equal $7$, we must also consider an additional scenario. All possible solutions for $a, b, $ and $n$ are presented in two tables, one for each case.

A hexapod robot's efficiency in various terrain scenarios can be assured by understanding the dynamics of individual legs. This research focuses on a monopod model with hydraulic legs interacting with a soft, deformable surface, inspired by a specific robot design. By simulating and analyzing the model, we identified areas for improvement. Initially, the model exhibited oscillatory behavior due to hydrocolloid surface interaction, leading to increased energy expenditure. To address this, the robot's design was modified by introducing two distinct leg types based on their functional roles. Results showed a significant reduction in energy consumption by about 24%. Furthermore, we explored the effects of surface softness, leg stiffness, and fluid viscosity on energy expenditure. These findings can be applied to the development of hexapod robots that can effectively navigate various surfaces.

In this paper, the authors develop a quasi-particle approach to describe the form factors of mesons in a unified framework, extending their previous work on particle masses. The form factors are determined by integrating the spectral functions of mesons, and the results are applied to the specific cases of scalar, vector, and axial vector mesons. The authors also derive general formulas for the electromagnetic and weak decay widths of these mesons. The predicted values for the form factors and decay widths are in line with previous findings from the quasi-particle approach, and the introduction of a new parameter "a" characterizes the particle-like behavior of quarks within mesons. The proposed method provides an alternative to the standard use of quark masses and condensates in QCD sum rules.

Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Current techniques represent pages on the web as flat constructs without consideration for the inherent hierarchical structure, which is actually present. This paper introduces a novel approach, Hierarchical Link Analysis (HiLA), a method for uncovering the hierarchical essence of web page relationships and inferring the underlying structure of information on the web. HiLA is a flexible framework that can be expanded upon and offers multiple optimization methods for large-scale applications. This approach is demonstrated through an analysis of search engine results page (SERP) data, specifically those related to question-answering platforms and web page classification.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the intersection of these two concepts and reveals that there exists a specific annealing interval, directly influencing solution finding and quench dynamics, which can be determined by analyzing the quantum system's long-tail behavior following a quench. Utilizing the quantum annealing optimizer for the exact cover problem as a case study, our findings demonstrate that the quench dynamics within the annealing interval exhibits distinct behavior compared to the outside region, which may impact solution-finding efficiency and provide a potential approach for enhancing the performance of quantum annealing.

Due to the lack of oxygen, the infinite layer nickelate $NCO$ exhibits strong screening, making it challenging to derive accurate values for nickel's effective charge and the energy of charged excitations within the parent compound's bandwidth. By combining the methods of asset-based extensions and effective models, our study develops a detailed understanding of screening and the electronic properties of $NCO$. We achieve this by converting the first-principles results from $NCO$ into a two-band model, allowing us to compare our findings with experimental data and identify key indicators of screening. Furthermore, we anticipate that heavy doping with oxygen will decrease the bandwidth of the upper band and shift the charge excitation energy, potentially leading to a more metal-like state in $doped $NiO$$_{1-x}O_y$.

The paper investigates the accuracy of relativistic mean-field models that incorporate a sigma field's influence on dense matter within compact stars. It is observed that these models overestimate the sigma field's impact, which in turn overestimates the matter's density at high densities. This overestimation results in the models failing to account for neutron stars' maximum possible mass. To circumvent this limitation, the paper suggests a alternative approach using the sound speed in matter rather than the sigma field's density. By doing so, it becomes possible to utilize the models while also incorporating uncertainties in nuclear matter's properties. Ultimately, the paper provides equations for sound speed in matter that can be used in models of neutron stars, including quark stars with strange matter.

We investigate a state with which a beam of light is described as being in a specific spatial pattern, specifically in regards to its phase structure and variability when compressed or displaced from its original form. Our research reveals that this state remains unchanged, maintaining its overall phase structure through both compression and displacement. However, when both compression and displacement are applied, our analysis shows that the state's phase structure does undergo a transformation, with the degree of change being influenced by the intensity of the state itself. Our study also examines the compressibility of this state under different compression techniques, with our results demonstrating a notable difference in state preservation outcomes. Our findings related to the compass state may be relevant to a broad range of optical systems that involve combining light beams in specific spatial patterns, with our research into compression techniques also potentially useful for interpreting physical phenomena in these systems.

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional.

Recent advancements in outsourcing training and machine learning as a service have created innovative threats such as hidden functionalities that are embedded in artificial neural networks. In typical research scenarios, triggers that activate these embedded features are static in their positioning and pattern, thus enabling detection mechanisms to function effectively. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and ABS to be vulnerable to triggers that are dynamic, meaning they are unaffected by pattern or location, thus compromising their reliability. What is even more challenging, is that these sophisticated backdoors require an inordinate amount of compromised training data. In a breakthrough study, it has been found that even without significantly compromising training data, hidden functionalities could arise from the presence of a specific neural network structure called the global mean pooling layer, despite initial difficulty in accomplishing this feat in various machine learning tasks such as sound classification, text sentiment analysis, and image classification.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. As satellite missions like Gaia provide increasingly precise parallax measurements, the potential impact of $\gamma$ variability on these calculations needs to be examined. By analyzing a model similar to that of Gaia, with a key difference being its ability to determine a non-standard value for $\gamma$, we found that varying $\gamma$ values significantly affect parallax estimates. In fact, a $\gamma$ deviation of 0.001 would result in a 0.023 mas change in the parallax measurement. Therefore, to minimize errors in parallax calculations, it's necessary to improve our understanding of the post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$.

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's practical to draw on a large existing question answer dataset. This approach leverages the existing knowledge encoded in trained language models to expand the scope of available expertise. Nonetheless, relying solely on existing data poses issues due to potential semantic errors, leading to questionable or unsafe answers. To address this challenge, we propose a novel strategy, Coarse-to-Careful, which begins by gathering a set of rough, less precise answers from a mixture of labeled instances. This coarse step serves to identify areas that likely contain semantic flaws without requiring complete annotation. A subsequent careful refinement phase aims to clarify these ambiguous cases by incorporating additional relevant labeled instances. A key component of the Coarse-to-Careful framework, a semantic-related assessment module, evaluates the coherence between the answer instances and candidate questions. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach for open-domain Commonsense Question Answering by incorporating the CC dataset, a new semantic-related question answer dataset. For further improvement, we advise combining the Coarse-to-Careful framework with strong pre-trained language models via training and inference.

Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, are rich in molecular cations whose exceptional brightness under UV to visible light can facilitate the understanding of local plasma environments and the composition of cometary neutral gas. Although optical spectra of these composite ions hold significant value, a notable lack of research exists on the spectrum of some common cations, most notably oxygen-based molecules, despite extensive studies of comet spectra. This article aims to fill this knowledge gap by providing a preliminary inventory of the composite ion spectrum, utilizing a combination of laboratory data and astronomical observations from three notable comets. The study focuses on cations containing only oxygen and other elements, and has been facilitated by the public release of vast amounts of spectral data from the Extreme Ultraviolet Spectrometer (EUVI) on the Solar-B satellite. The findings can be utilized by researchers to develop a more accurate interpretation of cometary spectra.

In the context of a small client with access to a limited amount of data seeking to train a machine learning model through federated learning, incorporating vast amounts of data from multiple untrustworthy sources is a critical challenge. While opthalmoscopic images hold considerable promise for automated diagnosis, they are similarly hampered by sources of varying quality. We present a novel approach, known as Stroll, that enables the client to explore the available sources effectively by selecting a subset that provides the most valuable information for model improvement. We also offer a circumventive method to accelerate learning through federated and heterogeneous data. We put Stroll through its paces on an authentic dataset of retinal images and show that it offers significant gains over existing methods.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders. An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system. The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not. The study found that offenders mandated to receive mental health treatment had a 9.5 percent lower chance of being reconvicted within a five-year period. The data suggests that forcing offenders to receive mental health treatment as part of their sentence leads to a lower risk of future criminal activity, despite initial concerns that requiring treatment could increase an offender's risk of future criminal activity.

A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper proposes a new regularization technique that enhances the consistency of unseen pixels in semi-supervised medical image segmentation. By applying this technique, previously unannotated pixels with similar characteristics will be labeled in the same region. This is achieved by dividing unannotated pixels into distinct regions based on low-dimensional feature spaces, which are learned through an auxiliary network. A novel loss function is introduced to ensure that unannotated pixels fall within established label boundaries, resulting in improved segmentation performance, particularly for finely structured objects. Evaluations using two publicly available datasets demonstrate the benefits of this approach over existing methods, particularly for segmenting intricate structures.

In a quantum mechanics framework, an operator's expectation value can be used to observe the behavior of a complex system dynamically. The expectation value of an operator is calculated using a density matrix, which represents the system's statistical state. As the system evolves over time, the density matrix and operator expectation values change in accordance with the Heisenberg picture. In this paper, we combine the Hamiltonian parameters and operator characteristics into a single, compact graph-based structure to track the evolution of the density matrix and operator expectation values. This structure enables efficient and accurate calculations throughout the system's dynamic progression. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach for both simple harmonic oscillators and the Bose-Hubbard model, with both local and nearest-neighbor interactions. Our results show that the graph-based method maintains high precision even at high chaos levels. We also develop a theoretical framework to analyze the algorithm's precision in relation to the system's chaos level.

Consider a parametric family of probability distributions defined by $P_y(\cdot|\theta)$, where $\theta$ is the parameter from the set $\Theta$, and a function $\eta:\Theta\to\mathbb{R}$ for which there are no known distributional assumptions. The goal of this research is to estimate the weighted average of parameters, $\eta(\theta)$, based on independent observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ with distributions $P_{X_1},\ldots,P_{X_n}$, where the weights add up to one. It is demonstrated that under specific smoothness conditions, the Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimator (GMLE) $\eta(\hat{\theta})$ where $\hat{\theta}=(\hat{\theta}_1,\ldld,\hat{\theta}_n)$ is an consistent estimator for the weighted average of parameters $\eta(\theta)$. Furthermore, the GMLE is shown to be asymptotically normal by establishing the differentiability of $\eta(\theta)$ and establishing that the Fisher information matrix is well defined and positive definite. The main application of this result is to the estimation of the average treatment effect in randomized controlled trials with partial participation, along the lines of imputed data analysis.

Knowledge tracing in educational settings involves predicting a student's correct or incorrect answer based on previously answered questions. Since the introduction of the Knowledge Tracing dataset by Klockler and Choi, this task has been frequently used as a benchmark in machine learning research. However, the original implementation of the knowledge tracing model is not readily available, forcing many researchers to rewrite the code. Furthermore, the original evaluation metrics are not publicly accessible, forcing researchers to recreate the dataset's original evaluation procedure manually. Both issues hinder comparisons between existing methods and potential future work. To address these challenges, we created pyKT, a Python-based library designed to ease the evaluation of deep learning knowledge tracing models and their comparison. pyKT provides an automated framework for evaluating knowledge tracing models, including multiple evaluation metrics and proxy labels to address cold start issues. We applied pyKT to existing knowledge tracing models, demonstrating its utility and highlighting opportunities for future research.

Given any real-analytic manifold $M$, we can define the space of elliptic differential operators acting on $M$. For a specific class of manifolds without boundary, namely those that are compactly grouped, we have proven that any differential operator defined on these manifolds is automatically elliptic. Now, let's consider a compact manifold $X$ that is parameterized by a compact space $S$ along with a pair of functions $F:\mathbb{R}^n\times S \to \mathbb{R}^n(n\geq 2)$ with non-degenerate determinant. We have shown that any differential operator that is invariant under the parameters and agrees with a known elliptic operator on the image under $F$ is also elliptic. Furthermore, we found that the range of these operators is closed when they act on functions defined on the image under $F$.

Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT's format for proof objects was introduced, aiming to bridge the gap between proof assistants and SMT solvers via translation paths. Since then, proof formats have evolved, and many solvers now offer alternative formats, albeit often solver-specific. In response to this trend, we present Alethe, a new proof format anticipated to accommodate various SMT solvers and cover different use cases. Alethe builds upon the fundamental principles of its predecessors while introducing novel features such as tagged terms and a more efficient encoding of substitution lists. We envision this format as a flexible foundation that can be tailored to suit the needs of applications connecting SMT solvers to proof assistants.

As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by allowing gradients to be submitted at any time, thus further increasing efficiency. However, allowing unrestricted gradients may lead to slow convergence, so we introduce an innovative method to adaptively adjust the duration of submission windows to balance efficiency and convergence. When data is not significantly changed over time, research shows that FedBuff with unrestricted gradients can be up to 2 times more efficient than traditional federated learning, and our algorithm achieves comparable performance to vanilla federated learning in various scenarios.

Recently, ASR systems have achieved high accuracy due to the advancement of large language models. However, training such models for low-resource languages is challenging because it requires a lot of data and a strong connection to the language structure. A promising approach to overcome this difficulty is language transfer, where a model is first trained on a high-resource language and then fine-tuned on the target language. Despite its success, current methods often fail to utilize a crucial advantage of many languages being translated into popular languages like English. In this paper, a new technique called CACTF is proposed to enhance ASR performance on low-resource languages by leveraging translated data in a high-resource language at two levels of fine-grained segmentation: first on the coarse level and then on the fine level. Furthermore, we explore whether this approach can be applied to ASR systems in high-resource languages directly. Experimental results on 12 low-resource languages and 3 high-resource languages show that CACTF achieves a significant improvement over the baseline models. In particular, it outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods by 8.13% and 5.59% in terms of word error rate on average, and also demonstrates comparable performance to systems specifically trained on much larger data sets, including 300K parameters full-fine-tuned model with a word error rate that is 9.85% lower than the baseline.

Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating through unknown environments by optimizing path planning based on reward feedback. By applying our method, robots can reduce learning time, expand feasible action spaces, and achieve more efficient route optimization. Our model uses Gaussian Process regression to create an efficient dynamic approximation of the value function, allowing for action selection using the upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm. We prove that our UCB selection scheme leads to a polynomial number of data points being collected to achieve near-optimal policies, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulated and real-world experiments involving navigation scenarios with reward signals and obstacles.

We employ a comprehensive anisotropic stress-energy tensor, defined by an irregular symmetrized tensor component and an orthogonal gradient of scalar field, to investigate general relativistic stellar objects. This analysis yields two key scenarios: one with a constant Beppo-Saccardi function, indicating a de Sitter spacetime boundary, and another with a variable Beppo-Saccardi function, representing an hyperbolic spacetime boundary. We then derive non-relativistic limits for both cases, which correspond to anisotropic and inhomogeneous stellar objects within Newtonian gravity, described by a polytropic equation of state.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, Domain Transfer GEC (DT-GEC), utilizing meta-learning to achieve efficient domain adaptation. Leveraging rich training data, we establish a strong foundation of error correction abilities that may be applied to a variety of unknown domains. In addition, we introduce a simple yet effective augmentation technique tailored to G ER E C. The proposed method achieves superior performance on three diverse GEC datasets, demonstrating the benefits of both linguistic knowledge acquisition and efficient adaptation. Specifically, DT-GEC outperforms strong baselines by 1.05 F score on the AWRE test set and demonstrates robust performance when compared to standard multi-task learning methods.

The task of allocating non-divisible items to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions are additive, has been extensively studied, yet the basic case where agents can make selfish, individual actions in response to allocations has not been thoroughly explored. In our research, we examine whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the ordering of players' actions, always produce equilibria that fairly distribute items based on agents' underlying values, given that valuations remain private. We define such mechanisms as being strongly fair. After introducing a useful representation of actions that simplifies analysis, we demonstrate the existence of strongly fair mechanisms for allocating items by proving that, in general, there exists a fair pricing that protects the integrity of all possible Nash equilibria, thereby making strong fairness a general property. Next, we investigate the specific case where agents' values can be represented by lotteries over single-item values, and show that, in this instance, a fair pricing that protects all possible Nash equilibria exists if and only if the distribution of values is symmetric. Finally, we discuss approaches to strengthening the notion of fairness and examine the relationship between our results and existing methods for establishing the existence of pure Nash equilibria in games with strategic agents.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of positive pion octet moments is conducted, incorporating two-current nucleon scattering processes to determine momentum distributions of quarks within pions. This analysis employs a lattice QCD dataset with symmetrical lattices size 2.45 fm by 6.85 fm, and a gauge link evolution method to eliminate volume effects. The results are then compared with traditional parton distribution functions, revealing that quark distributions within pions exhibit a distinct pattern of deviation from standard PDF assumptions. Specifically, this study finds that quark distributions in pions are generally altered in the high-momentum region, with results indicating that quark momentum distributions within pions exhibit an asymmetrical distribution of momentum in the x-direction, which cannot be accounted for by standard PDFs. Furthermore, this study finds a divergent result for the integral of isospin-breaking quark distributions when using the standard definition, which can be resolved by modifying the definition to yield a finite result. Lastly, the effects of volume isolation on quark momentum distributions are also examined, with results showing that even at the lattice spacing used, effects of isospin breaking on quark momentum distributions may not be entirely negligible.

Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
However, accurately using observed relations in this context is hampered by
not properly accounting for variations in mass accretion rates, a problem
especially prevalent in earlier stages of star formation. Conversely, we found
large-scale fluctuations in mass accretion rates of up to 2.5 dex for one
specific object, XX Cha, a well-studied young star with multiple line-of-sight
observing records. By combining data from various sources, we confirmed the
large-scale variability of mass accretion rates for XX Cha, with rates that
could reach as high as 10 ddots/day, a value typically seen for more
massive stars. This finding has significant implications for the appearance
of individual stars during low-mass star formation, and suggests that a
significant portion of apparently super-critical stars actually represent
relatively brief, high-accretion phases rather than persistent states. As such,
they may not be as commonly found as previously thought.

Offline learning for multiple agents via Reinforcement Learning holds significant
potential for developing robust policies without the need for extensive data.
However, learning from limited, potentially low-quality data is a major hurdle.
This research focuses on a fundamental aspect of offline multi-agent learning,
where agents can draw upon useful past actions to inform their current decision-making.
A key discovery made in this study is that, in offline settings, useful past actions
follow a specific pattern - specifically, they are often associated with favorable
outcomes.
Building upon this finding, the research develops a novel method called "Learning
from Good Paths" (LGP), which leverages this inherent structure to enhance the
quality of learned policies.
LGP is comprised of two main components: one identifies beneficial past actions
based on outcome indicators, while the other employs a multi-agent importance
sampling technique to select high-quality paths.
Thorough evaluation of LGP on multiple datasets demonstrates its capability to
produce superior results compared to existing offline multi-agent learning approaches.

We developed a novel approach for aligning MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional registration techniques rely heavily on manual initialization, due to megavoltage images' poor contrast, while our method leverages a limited number of reference points (RP's) to serve as both start and end points for the alignment process. A Convolutional Neural Network was used to overcome the challenge of limited training data, as usual. Aligning the images is viewed as a problem of manipulating the RP's, rather than the images themselves. We evaluated our algorithm in both 2D and 3D scenarios, utilizing actual treatment treatments, and measured its performance in terms of both image similarity and treatment delivery time. The results show that our algorithm can successfully treat patients in both 2D and 3D, with delivery times of 12min and 20min, respectively. Further optimization of the Convolutional Neural Network is expected to lead to faster treatment deliveries.

Quantum entanglement is a fundamental resource that enables various quantum applications, including metrology, secure communication, and computation. Entanglement within a system's subspace, particularly when it affects a single particle, has been extensively studied in the context of two-qubit interactions and has been found to influence the dynamics of coupled systems significantly. However, the impact of single-particle entanglement with multiple degrees of freedom was not thoroughly examined until now. Our research focuses on a specific, highly entangled state of a single oscillator and reveals that the entanglement's non-local character can result in genuine multi-location effects, a phenomenon we term multi-location steering. Moreover, our findings demonstrate that the amount of multi-location steering is directly proportional to the oscillator's entanglement density. Therefore, we establish a universal relationship between an oscillator's entanglement and its capacity for multi-location steering, thereby providing a specific example of a universal entanglement-based metric that yields meaningful physical consequences under two-qubit interactions.

The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and improved information systems within Internet of Vehicles (IoVs) has yielded substantial benefits, albeit with heightened risks of security breaches and compromised privacy. As IoVs technology continues to evolve, there's growing interest in privacy preservation methodologies that adapt to these changes. Federated Learning has shown promise in safeguarding IoVs data and addressing concerns about security and privacy, whereas Blockchain technology presents possibilities for secure and verifiable data management. This paper conducts an in-depth review of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs, exploring potential problems, viable solutions, and future directions. This comprehensive survey can serve as a foundation for developing novel BC-Enabled FL solutions to address various IoVs data privacy challenges and scenarios.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly three and a half days while the absence of the white dwarf spin frequency presents further evidence for a massive WD.  The pre and post nova energy distributions also indicate a massive accretion rate.  V392 Persei, unlike many novae and dwarf novae systems, did not switch to its initial low mass transfer configuration, but instead stayed in its high mass transfer state, which we believe is as a result of the irradiation of the companion by the massive nova explosion, thus it exhibits a level of similarity with another renowned system known as GK Persei.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to create codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then maps the GMM to a set of precoder codebooks based on the estimated density distribution. Only the parameters of the GMM are transmitted to the mobile terminal, allowing it to efficiently obtain a nearby precoder in the codebook by calculating the density distance. This results in reduced feedback bandwidth and computational load, and feedback termination can be implemented to prevent unnecessary feedback. Simulation environments simulate FDD systems and EVA scenarios, showing the proposed approach outperforms traditional methods with regard to throughput and feedback size.

Any lattice model can be converted into a multi-terminal nonequilibrium setup by adding appropriate hopping terms between different sites within a lattice. This process makes it possible to create strong fictitious gauge fields through nonequilibrium conditions. Our research focuses on the 3D Hofstadter-Tasaki model and reveals that its fictitious electric field can be highly resistant to changes in direction, with corresponding surface current patterns demonstrating remarkable stability. Unlike lower-dimensional scenarios, surface currents in this model exhibit distinct preferences for flowing along particular lattice planes. Our findings were achieved through numerical calculations and are supported by an analytical explanation utilizing Weyl semimetal theory. The resilience of surface currents in this model could be categorized into three distinct regimes based on the strength of the fictitious magnetic field, including a disordered phase, an ordered phase with multiple directions of preference, and a crystalline phase characterized by preferential alignment in only a single direction. The model's robust surface currents make it an ideal candidate for experimental demonstration of nonequilibrium effects and fictitious gauge fields in three-dimensional systems.

You et al. analyzed 12 years of LIGO-Virgo data from 2010 to 2022 and found no evidence for events like GW190521, which represents a merger of a massive neutron star and a black hole. By setting an upper limit on such a combination of mergers, they constrained the rate at which neutron stars are torn apart by black holes, specifically on the most massive class. For the most comprehensive dataset, they found this rate to be below 32.8 times per million solar masses per century. Additionally, they applied this insight to a model involving which stars can form neutron stars or be destroyed by black holes and obtained a similar limit on the number of stars that can form neutron stars per century, equivalent to 0.43 times the rate of supernovae explosions.

We examine the formation of supermassive black holes at the centers of massive galaxy bulges and nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model. This model allows us to identify the role of gas supply and the mass of the nuclear star cluster in forming massive black holes. Subsequent mergers of the black holes with neutron stars or other black holes are then modeled, and we consider their detection via gravitational waves. Specifically, we investigate the likelihood of identifying advanced black hole-neutron star or black hole-black hole merger events that result in the production of intermediate-mass black holes. Our analysis indicates that the majority of such events are detectable by LIGO and Virgo in the survey's current sensitivity, and future missions like LIGO+VI and CE. Furthermore, we find that a population of dwarf galaxies escapes detection, shedding light on the early universe and potentially illuminating the minimum mass of nuclear star clusters and the role of massive black holes in them.

In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. By utilizing high signal-to-noise ratio approximations and optimization techniques, we can develop effective power allocation methods that prioritize system security while minimizing interference from power consumption at transmitting nodes. Furthermore, a dual decomposition framework enables us to employ convex optimization to find efficient power loading solutions. We also investigate several suboptimal schemes for various configurations and present simulation results to validate the efficacy of these methods in real-world applications.

Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video identification tasks where large amounts of temporal data need to be processed. To overcome these constraints, we propose an algorithmic design that incorporates a new form of tensor decomposition called Hierarchical Tucker Decomposition (HTD). By leveraging this method, we significantly reduce the model's size while maintaining its performance. In addition, we developed a custom deep learning platform that integrates efficient HTD operations and accelerates computation by utilizing limited memory. To further optimize energy efficiency, we designed a low-precision data format that minimizes computation and memory usage. Experimental results show that LSTM networks using the HTD design outperform conventional tensor decompositions in terms of model size and performance, while also demonstrating excellent energy efficiency on our custom platform.

In a QFT, the expected value of a generic hermitian operator is determined by a convex combination of the vacuum states, using a probability distribution defined by the operator's two-point correlation function. This conviction has been challenged by certain counterexamples, yet it persists in many special situations, including those with symmetry protection and those involving a gravitationally induced operator, where its surrounding environment suggests it should behave similarly to a hermitian operator. Within a specific CFT, the average value of a globally defined hermitian operator can be calculated by integrating the operator's transformation properties over the conformal group, and it has been found that this integral yields a result that is not necessarily a convex combination of the vacuum states. Nevertheless, this non-convex result can be further simplified into a hermitian combination of the vacuum states, thereby upholding the original conviction. Moreover, this transformation provides a new perspective on the Feeble Gravity Conjecture, which proposed that in a specific CFT, the average value of a globally defined hermitian operator would behave as if it were surrounded by a weak gravitational field, and it appears that this conjecture holds true.

Given a Noetherian local ring with the property of being strongly F-regular, we establish an equivalence between two given conditions: that its tight Hilbert function reaches its maximum possible value at some degree, and the ring's depth is equal to its dimension.

An important challenge in designing policies to address concerns about auxiliary services like ride-hailing, online food delivery, and streaming, involves accurately estimating the effect of fees or regulations on companies'spending on these services. Current economic models, which consider a single firm operating in a fixed environment, are insufficient for guiding policy decisions, as they do not account for the complex interactions between companies in dynamic markets. In contrast, our Auxiliary Services Acquisition Model (ASA) utilizes a stylized example of two competing firms to explore the impact of fees, regulations, and other environmental factors on the services these companies provide. By incorporating feedback loops from market dynamics into the model, ASA provides a foundation for further research that can address more intricate market interactions, ultimately aiming to develop practical policy tools for guiding decisions in evolving environments.

This research investigates numbers that can be expressed as the sum of two distinct primes, and we term these numbers coprimble. We also examine numbers that are part of a prime-generating sequence, defined by $p_{n+1} = p_{n}^{2}+p_{n}$, where $p_{n}$ is a prime number. Our main findings related to these sequences include determining which coprimble numbers can be represented as the sum of two prime numbers, and identifying periodic patterns within the sequence of sums of two distinct primes.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be enclosed by a hexagonal shape, approximately 10 degrees of latitude in width, that developed in the same season and was likely formed by the combination of planetary and atmospheric conditions. This study reveals that the conditions necessary for the formation of polar vortices are more complex than previously thought and that a precise and detailed analysis of the processes occurring in the upper atmosphere of Saturn is essential.

This paper investigates solutions to the Schrödinger equation under nonlinear conditions, specifically within a region outside a compact convex obstacle where solutions are deemed explosive. We aim to extend existing proof from Kirchberg's work, originally applied to a single-dimensional scenario, to multiply dimensional cases.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

We create a linearization functor for full linearization that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis defines the image of the full linearization functor, resulting in a subcategory of k-fold vector bundles. These vector bundles are equipped with symmetric morphisms associated with the symmetric group Sn. A significant observation arises in the degree 2 scenario, where this added structure leads to the concept of symplectic double vector bundles. These have an opposite relationship with metric double vector bundles. The process of full linearization is also used to extend N-manifolds and a superizing construction.

This research focuses on providing an appropriate framework for defining the absolute value of certain complex-valued orbital integrals, initially introduced by M. Frenkel and A. Ortolanga as part of their work on unramifiedness for Hecke algebras associated with reductive algebraic groups over finite fields. Some key results, including a formula for calculating the square of an orbital integral, are obtained as consequences of a more general measure-related formula. Furthermore, the study establishes a connection between the measures resulting from certain geometric measures through conjugation and the measures obtained from orbital integrals, which facilitates the computation of certain Hecke algebra norms.

The success of axisymmetric binary neutron star mergers largely depends on the ability to distinguish between two possible outcomes: the immediate formation of a black hole or the formation of a neutron star with unusual properties. To achieve this, there is a critical need for a better understanding of how matter behaves under extremely high densities. While mergers generate an intense grid of electromagnetic radiation across the spectrum, revealing the stage of merger stages requires the ability to interpret large data sets efficiently. Our proposed approach involves using machine learning on a smaller set of large data, derived from realistic simulations of binary neutron star mergers, which includes a wide range of spectra across the neutron star temperature range. By focusing on a smaller feature set derived from a subset of the data, we can develop a practical method for predicting the stage of mergers based on spectral characteristics, and provide the foundation for a more comprehensive framework for predicting the stage of mergers based on a wide range of astrophysical parameters.

We introduce a novel mixed finite element method for single-phase Darcy flow within a media that contains a small number of fractures. These fractures are represented as higher-permeability channels within a more complex porous structure, and are distinguished by their significantly greater hydraulic conductivity. This method utilizes traditional bilinear finite elements for both the porous medium and fracture components, with particular constraints applied to the pressure gradient across each of these elements. This hybrid approach enables the model to accurately capture the behavior of fractures with arbitrary orientations, in comparison to more restrictive methods that require fractures to be aligned with specific finite elements. This method is further shown to promote computational stability when modeling fractures with significantly higher permeability than the surrounding porous medium.

Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a workflow that prioritizes rigorous testing of Bayes factor estimates and provides alternative methods for validation, along with a utility function for evaluating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates. We also introduce an open-source repository of Bayes factor estimates for cognitive science researchers to use and modify. Our goal is to create a transparent and reproducible framework for Bayes factor analysis that addresses the aforementioned complications and provides valuable insights for cognitive science researchers.

Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use.

We conduct a comprehensive landscape analysis of the fixed-rank matrix optimization problem under the Frobenius norm via a geodesic convexity perspective, leveraging a specific transportation cost. This analysis reveals the presence of highly complex local structures, including points of convexity degradation, singularities, and convex regions, which are not interconnected. Our findings significantly extend the current understanding of the landscape in a way that is directly applicable to important applications, including the well-known Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) and the optimization of a wide range of models in deep learning, by identifying areas of the landscape that behave non-convexly, including around the optimal solution and critical points far from the convex region. Our results are supported by a novel geodesic convex hull characterization that enables the identification of the geodesically convex region for any matrix decomposition problem. We also introduce a precise characterization of the geodesically convex hull under the fixed-rank optimization problem, which provides a new, non-trivial understanding of the landscape, supplemented by graphical and numerical examples illustrating its features.

A graph is considered bipartite if it can be divided into two distinct components: one featuring closed loops of an even length, and another comprising loops of various lengths. A graph is classified as cubic when each of its vertices is connected to exactly three edges. Building on previous unproven assumptions, it was proposed that cubic bipartite graphs require a minimum of five colors to properly color their edges. This submission aims to disprove that hypothesis by creating a robust edge-coloring model and applying it to demonstrate that a specific type of cubic bipartite graph, those with a particular loop structure, can be colored using just four colors.

We employed co-evolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning behavior and assess their capacity for convergence to a Nash Equilibrium. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions resulted in an ergodic Markov Chain, characterized by frequent occurrence of states leading to NE play in the stationary distribution. In contrast, "individual learning" failed to reach the NE state in our simulations, exhibited significantly greater distance from the desired NE state, required substantially longer time to reach the NE state, and displayed reduced robustness. Ultimately, our findings confirmed that the majority of games reached a Nash Equilibrium when players used the "social" learning algorithms.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. We establish in this study that the symbolic and typical power lengths of $I(\mathcal{D})$ are equivalent, with specific conditions under which they are also equal to the number of vertices in $\mathcal{D}$. Additionally, we determine the typical and symbolic powers required to obtain the radical of $I(\mathcal{D})$ as a factor of a specific ideal related to $\mathcal{D}$, which we call the oriented line graph ideal.

Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems will require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to explore the feasibility of a broader context-aware methodology for building reliability cases. In this example, we monitor specific output ranges to establish a foundation for a more comprehensive framework, which we call Context-Aware Reliable Neural Networks (CARRN). A case study with a mobile robot utilizes CARRN, demonstrating that a significant portion of its neural network can be reliably run with memory that is prone to errors. Our findings also highlight key challenges and potential solutions for future computer vision systems.

Building upon the Jordanian twist concept, we have derived a generalized version. The generalized version, modified in the $r$-symmetrized format, meets the requirements for a 2-cocycle. Additionally, we have obtained specific formulae for its associated star product and twisted coproduct. Furthermore, we have established that our generalized version is equivalent to a 1-cochain-derived twist from the basic Jordanian twist.

This paper introduces a novel framework for developing a unified semantic space that spans multiple languages. Unlike existing multi-lingual models, which combine languages by treating them as separate clusters, our approach merges languages into a single cluster to optimize the socio-economic efficiency of knowledge sharing. To achieve this, we reformulate the clustering objective to account for the structural consistency of word embeddings across languages. Furthermore, we extract representative semantic points from the unified semantic space that capture the intrinsic structure of the combined language cluster. These points serve as a compact, unified semantic representation that encompasses all included languages. Our results show that this unified representation outperforms separate monolingual models and serves as a strong pre-training platform for multi-lingual tasks.

The initial results of the study of the production of pions, kaons, protons, and phi mesons in Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV are reported based on ALICE data. The multiplicity of these particles at different collision centralities is investigated. The results show that the multiplicity of all particles increases with rising collision centrality. The ratio of the multiplicity of kaons to pions and the ratio of protons to pions are also determined and found to be consistent with previous findings in LHC Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV.

In late 2019, Chile underwent a significant social crisis, marked by extensive civil unrest, economic disruption, and the spread of vandalism. To effectively respond to this complex situation, authorities employed various strategies, including deploying military forces and shutting down internet access. To gain valuable insights, we developed a multi-agent model that simulates the reported patterns of vandalism over time, incorporating geographical factors and individual agents' actions. Unlike traditional models, our approach accounts for the non-local presence of agents, eliminating the need for a continuous agent density model. By adjusting several key variables, we obtained plausible results that resemble the reported vandalism patterns, albeit with some discrepancies. Our analysis suggests that reducing internet access may not significantly impact the progression of vandalism, while increasing military presence in hotspots can be an efficient and cost-effective strategy for managing civil unrest.

This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with exotic expression constraints, expanding traditional regular expressions with additive operators and fair to extend the capabilities for describing complex patterns of behavior in systems with concurrent interactions. Unlike conventional methods for containment assessment, this approach does not rely on converting expressions to equational definitions but instead employs existing tools for regular expression containment assessment and fair to determine containment relationships. A new method for solving differential inequalities with symbolic variables is also introduced to facilitate the containment analysis of exotic expression constraints. This method for containing exotic expression constraints is an important contribution in its own right and is particularly useful for extending the methods for containing regular expression constraints to include descriptors of system interactions with concurrent inputs.

This paper introduces EMA-VIO, a novel approach for deep visual-inertial localization with an external memory. It overcomes limitations of prior methods that rely heavily on motion estimates and rely on a limited internal memory for computation. Informed by observations of memory usage in neural networks, our approach leverages an external memory to enhance performance, yet we found it's actually beneficial to reduce external memory usage to take advantage of its structure for efficient computation. Further optimization is achieved by augmenting the model with attention mechanisms that prioritize relevant memory locations for computation. In our implementation of EMA-VIO, we utilize a small and low-latency visual network and inertial network with an external memory structure that facilitates efficient computation. Results show that EMA-VIO outperforms the current state-of-the-art VIO methods and demonstrates robust performance in challenging scenarios with mode transitions, despite the absence of dynamic map representation or motion smoothness constraints.

A new type of material, which we call "square-root Weyl materials," is proposed with a specific band structure containing critical points with dimension two and Weyl points as fundamentals. We envision these materials to be highly versatile in both their pure and doped forms, exhibiting unconventional electrical and magnetic properties, including nonlinear responses to electric fields, ferromagnetism, and unusual thermal and optical properties. A theoretical framework for inclusive analysis of these materials has been developed, offering a comprehensive understanding of their inherent properties and predicted behaviors under various modifications. Moreover, our theoretical model provides a practical path for realizing these materials in practice, offering guidelines for identifying the likely categories of square-root Weyl materials.

This study investigates the numerical solution to a linear inverse problem derived from Maxwell's equations, with the goal of reconstructing electric conductivity under the assumption of a frequency-independent dielectric constant. A quasi-reversibility approach is employed to overcome the difficulty of ill-posedness, and this method leads to a system of time-dependent Maxwell's equations with initial conditions that can be numerically solved using a finite element method. Computational results are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of this numerical strategy.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Collection (FEDISC) problem, a new approach to assembling global knowledge from disparate sources.
